We appreciate your thoughtful follow-up. Regarding Q3, the sensor failures that inspired our pretraining scheme come from prior research in broader sensor domains, including NASA’s studies on sensor faults in aerospace applications [Balaban et al., 2009] and wireless sensor networks (e.g., for environmental monitoring) [Jesus et al., 2017]. While our primary focus of the evaluation is VSA estimation for driving, the sensor failure types that we simulate, such as bias, noise, scaling, and hard faults, are not specific to driving and are common across different physical sensors.

We included the Beijing PM10 dataset to show that robustness gains from our pretraining scheme extend to a different domain beyond driving. However, the experiments in the paper do not support your stronger claim that “the presented pretraining schema should be applicable to sensory data in general”, since we do not consider modalities such as images and LiDAR point clouds. Nevertheless, we believe that (1) the sensor failure types considered by our pretraining scheme reflect a wide range of sensor faults in diverse applications (as inspired by [Balaban et al., 2009] and [Jesus et al., 2017]), and that (2) our experiments on VSA estimation on a public dataset with simulated sensor failures, VSA estimation for closed-loop autonomous racing on a 2019 Lexus LC 500, and air quality level prediction on the Beijing PM10 dataset, demonstrate the robustness and generality of the proposed pretraining scheme in diverse domains with faulty sensory data.

We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback, valuable questions, and positive assessment of the paper’s clarity and experimental design.

### **Weaknesses**:

**W1 and Q1**: Thank you for the suggestion. We agree that comparing against recent time-series pretraining methods offers valuable insight, especially regarding nominal performance and robustness.

Our primary goal was to isolate the effect of adapting the pretraining task to handle sensor failures, rather than to outperform the best nominal models. To do this, we used the same architecture with and without robustness-focused masking, emphasizing the impact of our approach. Most existing methods, such as Sim-MTM and Ti-MAE, do not explicitly address robustness or sensor outages.

Nonetheless, we conducted additional experiments with Sim-MTM. Since it was originally evaluated on classification and forecasting, we adapted it for the state estimation setting. While Sim-MTM performs well under nominal conditions, our method shows superior performance under sensor outages, underscoring the value of robustness-aware pretraining. A summary of results is provided below, with full details to be included in the appendix of the paper. The table shows the MSE of the lateral velocity estimation (as in Fig. 3), averaged across all failing sensors for a specific failure mode.

**Comparison of Our Method vs. SimMTM Across Failure Types**

| Failure Type | Ours     | SimMTM  |
|--------------|----------|---------|
| Bias         | **0.0484*** | 0.1352  |
| Mean         | **0.0536*** | 0.1203  |
| Noise        | **0.0283*** | 0.0423  |
| Scaling      | **0.0433*** | 0.1009  |
| No failure   | **0.0259*** | 0.0400  |

\* Lowest error per row marked in bold.

Sim-MTM was evaluated using the original paper’s recommended hyperparameters. While further tuning might boost nominal performance (improving the absolute errors), we don’t expect significant gains in robustness, as the method isn’t designed for such scenarios. We hope this also addresses Question 1 sufficiently. 

We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and believe these additions strengthen the paper.

**W2 and Q3**: Robust sensor representations could benefit a range of tasks beyond VSA estimation, such as traction control (e.g., estimating wheel slip), road condition monitoring (e.g., classifying wet or icy surfaces), and tire or brake wear estimation. In general, our approach might be applicable to many sensors whose signal might degrade or be missing, including ride height sensors or pushrods in race cars, and position estimation with satellite information.

We chose VSA estimation because it is a well-established and challenging task in the literature, making it an effective and communicable benchmark. It also plays a central role in understanding vehicle dynamics. We will clarify this in the experiment section.

In response to your comment, we conducted additional experiments on the Beijing PM10 dataset from the Time Series Extrinsic Regression (TSER) benchmark. This dataset involves predicting PM10 air quality levels in Beijing based on various environmental measurements, such as pollutant concentrations, temperature, and pressure. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method drastically improves robustness to sensor failures in this setting. For comparison, we report the XGBoost RMSE from the TSER benchmark website, which represents the strongest performance on the dataset under standard (non-failure) conditions.

**Beijing PM10 Benchmark - Mean RMSE ± Std across Sensor Failures**

| Error Type   | Baseline         | PT Baseline      | Ours              | XGBoost (RSER BM) |
|--------------|------------------|------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| bias         | 117.63 ± 21.06   | 127.22 ± 27.48   | **104.89 ± 6.29*** | -                 |
| mean         | 107.41 ± 12.36   | 103.29 ± 3.68    | **101.07 ± 5.21*** | -                 |
| noise        | 98.19 ± 6.92     | 108.20 ± 6.78    | **97.52 ± 2.59***  | -                 |
| scaling      | 359.13 ± 756.87  | 402.42 ± 843.38  | **117.44 ± 27.10***| -                 |
| no_failure   | 95.06            | 97.98            | 94.05              | **93.13***        |

\* Lowest error per row marked in bold.

Our method enhances robustness to sensor failures in the driving domain and clearly improves robustness in estimating air quality in the Beijing PM10 dataset. Its general applicability to other domains remains an open question, which we plan to explore in future work. In response to your concern, we will add an evaluation with the additional benchmark in the appendix. We hope this also addresses Question 3 sufficiently.
### **Questions**:

**Q2**: This is a very good suggestion. Relevant linear imputation methods familiar to the authors hinge on knowing where data is missing. In our application, this is not known, and would necessitate non-trivial fault detection schemes.

Kalman filters (KFs) are more readily applicable, but make several strict assumptions, such as Gaussian i.i.d. noise statistics and the absence of unmodeled disturbances on the measurements. The sensor failures that we are considering violate both of these assumptions and can lead to significant performance degradation in the estimates.

To illustrate this, we run a KF on the data from the real-time experiments in Fig. 6. To implement the KF, we need to assume knowledge of a carefully tuned physics model, where the sideslip angle is a state and observable in measurements of longitudinal velocity, yaw rate and rear wheel speeds. For this purpose, we use bicycle dynamics with a Fiala tire model. We then implement a nonlinear KF and estimate the side slip angle using the disturbed wheel speeds in the experiment in Fig. 6. We obtain the following average and maximum errors in its reconstruction.

| Method                   | RMSE     | MAE     |
|--------------------------|----------|---------|
| Baseline (no pretraining)| 0.047    | 0.462   |
| KF (w/ physics model)    | 0.018    | 0.170   |
| Proposed (w/ pretraining)| **0.006*** | **0.030*** |

\* Lowest error per column marked in bold.

Despite not having access to the physics-based motion model, the proposed pretraining method yields better reconstruction results. We will include these additional experiments with details on the implemented KF and the vehicle model in the appendix of the final version, and thank the reviewer for suggesting the comparison.

We thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback, for recognizing the relevance of our approach in the autonomous driving setup, and for raising important questions regarding its assumptions and generalizability.
### **Weaknesses**:

**W1**: We would like to clarify that Sec. 3.1 describes a set of general sensor outages, building on a body of work from NASA [Balaban et al., 2009] and a work about wireless sensor networks [Jesus et al., 2017], distinct from our driving application. Training with these finite general failures improves sensor outage robustness in driving, and we speculate that it could bring improvements in other domains, such as GNSS positioning (where multi-path effects are present).

1) To test the generalizability of our model, we evaluated it on the previously unseen failure mode of "scaling," demonstrating that the model better generalizes to novel sensor faults not seen during training (Sec. 5.1).
2) Additionally, in experiments not reported in the paper, we replaced some vehicle signals with data from an external Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) with different noise statistics and biases to the signals in the training data. Here too, the reconstruction was of good enough quality to permit closed-loop control on the estimated sideslip angle in the presence of input disturbances similar to those in Fig. 6.

In response to your comment and to strengthen our evaluation, we conducted additional experiments on the Beijing PM10 dataset from the Time Series Extrinsic Regression (TSER) benchmark. This dataset involves predicting PM10 air quality levels in Beijing based on various environmental measurements, such as pollutant concentrations, temperature, and pressure. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method also improves robustness to sensor failures in this setting. For comparison, we report the XGBoost RMSE from the TSER benchmark website, which represents the strongest performance on the dataset under standard (non-failure) conditions.

**Beijing PM10 Benchmark - Mean RMSE ± Std across Sensor Failures**

| Error Type   | Baseline         | PT Baseline      | Ours              | XGBoost (RSER BM) |
|--------------|------------------|------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| bias         | 117.63 ± 21.06   | 127.22 ± 27.48   | **104.89 ± 6.29*** | -                 |
| mean         | 107.41 ± 12.36   | 103.29 ± 3.68    | **101.07 ± 5.21*** | -                 |
| noise        | 98.19 ± 6.92     | 108.20 ± 6.78    | **97.52 ± 2.59***  | -                 |
| scaling      | 359.13 ± 756.87  | 402.42 ± 843.38  | **117.44 ± 27.10***| -                 |
| no_failure   | 95.06            | 97.98            | 94.05              | **93.13***        |

\* Lowest error per row marked in bold.

Our method enhances robustness to sensor failures in the driving domain and clearly improves robustness in estimating air quality in the Beijing PM10 dataset. Its general applicability to other domains remains an open question, which we plan to explore in future work. In response to your concern, we will clarify point 1), and include a discussion of point 2) along with an evaluation with the additional benchmark in the appendix.

**W2**: Thank you for the suggestion, and we agree that the composite failure setting is both interesting and valuable to study.

We focused on individual sensor failures to isolate their effects on sensor outage robustness. However, our pretraining process does include composite failures. The masking strategy used during pretraining samples multiple sensor dropouts per sequence (see Sec. 4.1), and the model is trained under composite failure conditions, and therefore, to a certain extent, robust to several simultaneous sensor failures.

To directly address your comment and improve the evaluations, we conducted new experiments evaluating performance under composite failures at test time. We randomly select 1 to 4 sensors to fail in parallel and evaluate 10 configurations per failure count, to reflect the fact that certain sensor combinations can be more detrimental than others. Below, we report the average MSE under 10 different coupled sensor failure configurations - tested on 1-4 simultaneous failures.

**Performance Across Coupled Sensor Failures**

| Failing Sensors | Baseline | Baseline PT | Baseline Ours |
|------------------|----------|--------------|----------------|
| 1                | 0.1037   | 0.0920       | **0.0443***     |
| 2                | 0.1775   | 0.1831       | **0.0994***     |
| 3                | 0.1386   | 0.1866       | **0.0843***     |
| 4                | 0.2525   | 0.2244       | **0.1430***     |

\* Lowest error per row marked in bold.

Our method consistently improves robustness compared to the zero-masking baseline (except in the case of pure mean-value outages) across nearly all composite failure settings. As the number of failing sensors increases, all models naturally degrade in performance, but the proposed method consistently improves performance over the baselines in the other composite failure setting.

We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and will include the full evaluation setup and extended results in the appendix of the final version.

**W3**: Our approach shares the goal of improving robustness, but differs from domain randomization in two key respects:

1) Data source: Domain randomization typically perturbs simulated environments by randomizing physical or visual parameters. Our method applies structured corruptions to real-world data to mimic sensor failure modes, and is thus closer to data augmentation.
2) Goal and training objective: Domain randomization is often used to train models that are robust to distribution shifts in downstream tasks (e.g., locomotion across varied terrains). Our approach uses a self-supervised pretraining scheme that explicitly trains the model to recover original signals from fault-corrupted inputs. This aligns more closely with denoising and masked modeling approaches than traditional domain randomization.

While different, the two approaches are complementary and could be combined to further improve robustness. Additionally, we will clarify the distinction in the related work section by adding a paragraph about data augmentation.

**W4**: We agree that with knowledge of failure modes probability or the downstream task and how various errors will affect it, we could tune or learn the weights on the different failure modes as you suggest. For generality's sake, we decided not to fine-tune the loss function in Eq. (3) to the downstream control objective. As reported in the response to W1, using the same loss yields significant robustness benefits in a radically different application of predicting air quality. While it would be interesting to investigate the impact of the weights in the loss in future work, current results already show significant improvements in robustness compared to prior work without bespoke tuning of the loss.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive and encouraging feedback, particularly regarding the significance and originality of our work. We also appreciate the constructive questions and suggestions aimed at improving the clarity and presentation of the paper.
### **Questions**:

**Q1 & Q4**: Thank you for the suggestion. We chose to include Figures 1 and 2 early in the paper to serve as a kind of graphical abstract, providing readers with a quick visual overview of the main ideas and results. However, we recognize the potential disruption this placement may cause to the narrative flow, as you pointed out. We will move their location in the final manuscript to improve the clarity of the presentation.

**Q2**: Sec. 3.1 describes a set of general sensor outages, building on a body of work from NASA [Balaban et al., 2009] and a work about wireless sensor networks [Jesus et al., 2017], distinct from our driving application. We neglected faults that manifest as NaN values, which we view as a practical variant of the hard fault already described. Additionally, we excluded time-series anomalies like flipped seasonality, as they are not directly caused by sensor faults.

**Q3**: Yes, that is correct. We refer to the uniform distribution over the interval [l,u]. We will revise the text to make this notation explicit and avoid any ambiguity.

**Q5**: Thank you for pointing this out. The notations are intended to represent the same value, and we will make the notation consistent throughout the manuscript to improve its clarity.

**Q6**: The overhead images are constructed using positional data and drone footage. We overlaid a car image to indicate driving direction, but since we didn’t record every trial with a drone, the car position is fixed. The trajectory (purple line) is the key data point, but we agree that the static car image may be a bit misleading and will clarify this in the figure caption.

We thank the reviewer for the detailed feedback, and for highlighting the novelty of our pretraining strategy and the strength of our empirical results, as well as for the constructive suggestions for improvement.
### **Weaknesses**:

**W1 & Q1**: Due to the combinatorial complexity of covering all 10 failure modes and their combinations, we focused on three representative types informed by our experience with VSA in the driving domain - bias, noise, and hard fault. All combinations of these three failure types were systematically evaluated (see Appendix C).

Bias masking was chosen to approximate several untested faults: short, sharp offsets during training mimic outliers, while drift, trimming, and scaling resemble varying bias over time. Given our short sequence lengths, we assume minimal temporal dynamics, making a static bias a reasonable proxy. Our evaluation of the holdout scaling fault supports this, showing effective generalization. For domains with lower sampling rates or longer sequences, including additional fault types in pretraining could be beneficial. We hope this also addresses Question 1 sufficiently.

You raise a very good point, and we will clarify this in the paper.

**W2**: Thank you for the suggestion. We agree that comparing against recent time-series pretraining methods offers valuable insight, especially regarding nominal performance and robustness.

Our primary goal was to isolate the effect of adapting the pretraining task to handle sensor failures, rather than to outperform the best nominal models. To do this, we used the same architecture with and without robustness-focused masking, emphasizing the impact of our approach. Methods, such as Sim-MTM and Ti-MAE, do not explicitly address sensor outage robustness in their pretraining procedure.

Nonetheless, we conducted additional experiments with Sim-MTM. Since it was originally evaluated on classification and forecasting, we adapted it for the state estimation setting. While Sim-MTM performs well under nominal conditions, our method shows superior performance under sensor outages, underscoring the value of robustness-aware pretraining. A summary of results is provided below, with full details to be included in the appendix of the paper. The table shows the MSE of the lateral velocity estimation (as in Fig. 3), averaged across all failing sensors for a specific failure mode.

**Comparison of Our Method vs. SimMTM Across Failure Types**

| Failure Type | Ours     | SimMTM  |
|--------------|----------|---------|
| Bias         | **0.0484*** | 0.1352  |
| Mean         | **0.0536*** | 0.1203  |
| Noise        | **0.0283*** | 0.0423  |
| Scaling      | **0.0433*** | 0.1009  |
| No failure   | **0.0259*** | 0.0400  |

\* Lowest error per row marked in bold.

Sim-MTM was evaluated using the original paper’s recommended hyperparameters. While further tuning might boost nominal performance, we don’t expect significant gains in robustness, as the method isn’t designed for such scenarios.

We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and believe these additions strengthen the paper.

**W3 & Q3**: We would like to clarify that Sec. 3.1 describes a set of general sensor outages, building on a body of work from NASA [Balaban et al., 2009] and a work about wireless sensor networks [Jesus et al., 2017], distinct from our driving application. Training with these finite general failures improves sensor outage robustness in driving, and it could bring improvements in other domains, such as GNSS positioning (where multi-path effects are present).

In response to your comment, we conducted additional experiments on the Beijing PM10 dataset from the Time Series Extrinsic Regression (TSER) benchmark. This dataset involves predicting PM10 air quality levels in Beijing based on various environmental measurements, such as pollutant concentrations, temperature, and pressure. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method drastically improves robustness to sensor failures in this setting. For comparison, we report the XGBoost RMSE from the TSER benchmark website, which represents the strongest performance on the dataset under standard (non-failure) conditions.

**Beijing PM10 Benchmark - Mean RMSE ± Std across Sensor Failures**

| Error Type   | Baseline         | PT Baseline      | Ours              | XGBoost (RSER BM) |
|--------------|------------------|------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| bias         | 117.63 ± 21.06   | 127.22 ± 27.48   | **104.89 ± 6.29*** | -                 |
| mean         | 107.41 ± 12.36   | 103.29 ± 3.68    | **101.07 ± 5.21*** | -                 |
| noise        | 98.19 ± 6.92     | 108.20 ± 6.78    | **97.52 ± 2.59***  | -                 |
| scaling      | 359.13 ± 756.87  | 402.42 ± 843.38  | **117.44 ± 27.10***| -                 |
| no_failure   | 95.06            | 97.98            | 94.05              | **93.13***        |

\* Lowest error per row marked in bold.

Our method enhances robustness to sensor failures in the driving domain and clearly improves robustness in estimating air quality in the Beijing PM10 dataset. Its general applicability to other domains remains an open question, which we plan to explore in future work. 

1) To test the generalizability to unseen sensor errors, we evaluated it on the previously unseen failure mode of "scaling," demonstrating that the model better generalizes to novel sensor faults not seen during training (Sec. 5.1).
2) Additionally, in experiments not reported in the paper, we also tested our method on a race track, where the vehicle was driven at higher speeds and encountered more dynamic conditions. While the skidpad setup is more reflective of regular driving, the race track introduces racing-like scenarios with increased complexity and variability. Our method showed comparable robustness in both settings, suggesting its ability to scale beyond structured environments. We focused on the skidpad in the paper due to its higher reproducibility and clearer communicability, but the track results provide additional support for real-world applicability.

In response to your concern, we will add the additional benchmark and a discussion of point 2) to the appendix, and will clarify point 1) in the main text. We hope this also addresses Question 3 sufficiently.
### **Questions**:

**Q2**: Early hyperparameter studies showed that a 10% masking ratio, paired with an average mask length matching the input sequence length, offers the best trade-off between robustness and downstream performance. Nearby values (e.g. 15%) showed only minor degradation. We speculate that this choice prevents simple interpolation and encourages the model to learn cross-channel dependencies. It may also help simulate outlier scenarios by occasionally masking parts of other channels. For intuition, with an input of 220 scalars (sequence length × features), a 10% masking ratio results in 22 masked data points, with one channel being completely masked on average.

We show that too-small bias bounds during pretraining hurt performance under strong offset and scaling errors, likely due to the inputs deviating too far from the training distribution. Using bias levels up to three standard deviations improves robustness (see Appendix G).

Finally, we find that while noise level effects are less pronounced, too little noise during pretraining still leads to degraded robustness. A moderate amount of noise helps the model generalize to noisier test conditions (see Appendix H).

**Q4**: This is a very good suggestion. Early experiments using the pretraining reconstruction head as an anomaly detector showed promise but were ultimately left out of the paper. Extending this to classify outage types is a strong direction for future work, as it may provide additional actionable information for downstream tasks and diagnostics.

summary.value: This paper introduces a self-supervised pretraining approach for multivariate time series aimed at enhancing robustness against realistic sensor failures. Unlike conventional methods that use simple zero-masking, this work simulates specific failure modes such as bias, noise, and hard faults during pretraining. The goal is to encourage the model to reconstruct the original signal despite these complex corruptions. The approach is evaluated on vehicle dynamics data for sideslip angle estimation, where it demonstrates improved robustness on both seen and unseen test tracks. Furthermore, it is deployed in a real-world autonomous racing scenario, successfully enabling stable closed-loop control even when sensor faults are intentionally injected.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
# strength
1. Problem Significance: The paper addresses the important and practical problem of safety-critical sensor failures, which is highly relevant for real-world systems like autonomous vehicles.

2. Novel Pretraining Strategy: The proposal to use masking methods that are grounded in realistic sensor faults (e.g., bias, noise) is a clear strength over standard mean-only masking.

3. Strong Empirical Results: The experimental results, on both synthetic data and a real-world application, clearly demonstrate the robustness of the proposed masking approaches (bias, noise, and mean) compared to a standard mean-only masking baseline. The successful deployment in a closed-loop autonomous racing scenario is a particularly strong piece of evidence.

4. Thorough Ablation Studies: The paper provides valuable ablation analyses that examine the effects of different masking strategies, failure intensities, model sizes, and the model's ability to generalize to unseen fault conditions.

# weakness
1. Incomplete Evaluation of Fault Modes: The primary weakness is that the experiments do not cover all seven fault modes listed in Section 3.1 (e.g., drift, outliers). The mapping between the three tested masking techniques (mean, bias, noise) and the seven real-world failure modes is only described qualitatively. For example, the assumption that bias corruption is sufficient to model sensor drift is not empirically validated, leaving the model's robustness to these other modes unclear.

2. Limited Baselines: The comparison is limited to a non-pretrained baseline and a simple mean-only masking baseline. The evaluation would be significantly stronger if the proposed method were compared against other state-of-the-art time-series pretraining and masking methods (e.g., Ti-MAE, Sim-MTM).

3. Questionable Generalizability: The evaluation focuses on a single application domain (vehicle dynamics). This concentration, while providing a strong case study, limits the evidence for the method's generalization to other multivariate time series settings (e.g., healthcare, industrial IoT) which may have different fault characteristics. Additionally, the real-world tests are confined to controlled racing environments, making it unclear how the method would scale to more diverse and unstructured contexts.

questions.value:
1. Could you provide a more systematic analysis or justification for why the pretraining was based on only three of the seven identified fault modes? Is there empirical evidence to show that the chosen masking strategies (bias, noise, hard fault) can effectively represent the other un-tested failure types like drift and outliers?

2. How robust is the method to changes in the pretraining hyperparameters, such as the masking ratio, the bounds set for bias injection, and the levels of noise?

3. How do you see this approach transferring to other time series domains, such as health monitoring or industrial IoT, where sensor outage characteristics might be significantly different?

4. Given that the model is trained to reconstruct signals from specific fault types, could this pretraining strategy also be leveraged to detect or classify which failure mode is present at test time, in addition to improving robust estimation?

summary.value: This paper proposes a self-supervised masking method to learn how to recover timeseries signals from common sensor faults. Specifically, the authors propose an encoder-based model that is pretrained on masked data that incorporates three common corruptions: mean masking, constant biasing, and Gaussian noising. Then, the encoder is fixed and the decoder is finetuned for the downstream task at hand. The proposed method is evaluated in simulation using a vehicle dataset, and it is shown that the proposed method achieves lower reconstruction error than the baselines (either with no pretraining, or with pretraining using only mean masking), indicating a higher degree of robustness against the sensor faults at hand. In the simulation, it is also shown that the proposed method achieves better reconstruction than the baselines in the case of unseen sensor faults (that is, scaling faults, which were not incorporated in the pretraining). The model is also demonstrated on an actual autonomous vehicle experiment, where it is shown to yield reconstruction estimates good enough to result in stable closed-loop vehicle control, whereas the baseline method either led to the vehicle leaving the track or needing human interference.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Quality: Overall, this is a high-quality and complete piece of work, with technically sound approaches and evaluations. The evaluation of the proposed method is thorough, with plenty of ablation studies provided. No theoretical developments or claims are made, so all of the support provided is empirical. The authors are transparent about the limitations of their work (dedicating the entire Section 6 to describe limitations and possible future work to overcome such limitations).

For the most part, the paper is formatted and structured well (see my enumerated "Questions" below for specific questions and suggestions on how to improve the clarity and presentation). The literature review is relatively thorough, giving the reader a good idea of recent relevant work. Enough data, code, and experimental descriptions are provided (with much of it in the appendices and supplement) to reproduce the results.

Significance: The problem considered is an important one; indeed, it is necessary for safety-critical autonomous systems to be resilient against sensor faults and timeseries data corruptions, especially as control systems become more dependent on learning-based methods. The paper does not provide any theoretical analysis of the proposed model, which would certainly boost the significance of the work, as it is also important to grant safety-critical systems provable reliability and robustness guarantees. final_justification.value: I thank the authors for their responses to my questions/suggestions, and for clarifying/fixing the potentially misleading aspects of the overhead images. I have also read through the other reviews and responses, and I am happy to see the authors have performed a handful of additional comparisons to baselines and ablation studies, all in support of their proposed methods. summary.value: This paper proposes a self-supervised pretraining approach to improve the robustness of a model against real-world sensor faults, focusing on an autonomous driving setup. Instead of a generic masking strategy, the authors consider a set of failure modes and devise a fault-aware masking strategy to address these. The approach is evaluated on a real autonomous driving system (Lexus LC 500), considering various failure modes.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

1. Considering a fault-aware masking strategy appears effective for handling the domain-specific scenarios.

2. The authors consider a set of real-world failure modes that are relevant to the autonomous driving setup.  

3. The approach demonstrates effectiveness in a real autonomous driving system (Lexus LC 500).

4. Evaluations consider known and unseen tracks, ablations, and sensitivity analysis of the approach.


Weaknesses:

1. The approach assumes the failure modes are known in advance. This may be appropriate in specific domains, but mostly does not hold in practical scenarios. 

2. How about composite failures? Can the pretraining on individual mode handle the situations while multiple sensor failures occur at the same time?

3. How is the proposed approach fundamentally different from domain randomization, which is commonly used to adapt to novel scenarios in robotics? 

4. The loss function (equ. 3) imposes an equal weight to all failure modes. However, in real-world scenarios, this might not be the case as failures are evaluated based on their impacts.

questions.value: Please address the comments in the weaknesses section.

value: NO or VERY MINOR ethics concerns only

final_justification.value:
Thanks for conducting the additional experiments and providing additional results. I do appreciate the effort.

While the numbers show the approach can handle some of the novel failures, I fail to understand what aspect of the approach allows this capability. There is no explicit mechanism to address novel failures.

Similarly, even though the experiments show that some of the composite failures can be handled, it is not what enables this. As the augmentations are made independently, and the loss function is a linear combination of the individual losses, the ability to capture composition is limited.

I was hoping to see some technical reasoning for these two scenarios. Experimental results alone may not be sufficient, as we don't know how orthogonal or similar the failures are. As these are crucial for real-world applications, I stick to the original score.

summary.value: The paper presents a reconstruction pretraining schema for car sensory data which uses different sensor failures to mask the inputs. The goal is to achieve representations that are more robust towards such sensor failures. They test their approach on two vehicle sideslip angle (VSA) estimation tasks: an open-source data set and a real-world autonomous driving setting. They compare against no pretraining and traditional mean masking pretraining and determine that their approach achieves substantially more robust and thus accurate results.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths:** 

**S1** The paper is very well written in terms of quality and clarity. As somebody who is not extensively familiar with the autonomous driving domain, the paper gave the right overview of different sensor failures and why they are important. 

**S2** The perturbation strategy is well-argued and seems to work well for robust representations of car sensory data. The ablation studies are extensive. 

**S3** The evaluation of the approach is done on an open-source data set, which is beneficial for recreating the results, and in an autonomous driving scenario, underscoring its transferability to real-world applications (even though the car drives in a relatively simple circle). 

**Weaknesses:** 

**W1** Both baselines are either relatively weak (no pretraining) or a subset of the proposed pretraining approach (mean masking).  Another pretraining method for time series data such as e.g. SimMTM [1] would be a stronger baseline.

**W2** The evaluation, while extensive, focuses only on one task: VSA estimation. 

[1] Dong, J., Wu, H., Zhang, H., Zhang, L., Wang, J., & Long, M. (2023). Simmtm: A simple pre-training framework for masked time-series modeling. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 36, 29996-30025.

questions.value:
**Q1** Why did you not compare yourself against other time series pretraining methods like SimMTM? 

**Q2** How does your approach compare against more traditional methods like linear imputating the failed sensor value or Kalman Filtering of all sensor data? 

**Q3** What other tasks besides VSA estimation would benefit from more robust sensor representations in (autonomous) driving? And why did you choose VSA estimation as the sole evaluation task in this paper?

If all three questions are answered adequately, meaning to be either argued as non-significant or respective additions to the manuscript are made, I am willing to increase my score to accept.

final_justification.value:
Questions Q1 and Q2 are answered sufficiently and provide comparison baselines that do not specifically train for more robust representations. 

In terms of Q3, the authors included an air quality dataset. I can not comment on how comparable sensory failures modes for autonomous driving and air quality measurement are and if these two applications are representable applications for the sensory data domain in general. But I value the inclusion of a different domain dataset to showcase the generalisability of the method. However, I would suggest the authors to focus either only on the autonomous driving domain or, if claiming more broader generalisability, argue why their evaluations cover all relevant types of sensor data. As I am no expert in this domain, I will keep my score.

title.value: From Faults to Features: Pretraining to Learn Robust Representations against Sensor Failures

abstract.value:
Machine learning models play a key role in safety-critical applications, such as autonomous vehicles and advanced driver assistance systems, where their robustness during inference is essential to ensure reliable operation. Sensor faults, however, can corrupt input signals, potentially leading to severe model failures that compromise reliability. In this context, pretraining emerges as a powerful approach for learning expressive representations applicable to various downstream tasks. Among existing techniques, masking represents a promising direction for learning representations that are robust to corrupted input data. In this work, we extend this concept by specifically targeting robustness to sensor outages during pretraining. We propose a self-supervised masking scheme that simulates common sensor failures and explicitly trains the model to recover the original signal. We demonstrate that the resulting representations significantly improve the robustness of predictions to seen and unseen sensor failures on a vehicle dynamics dataset, maintaining
strong downstream performance under both nominal and various fault conditions. As a practical application, we deploy the method on a modified Lexus LC 500 and show that the pretrained model successfully operates as a substitute for a physical sensor in a closed-loop control system. In this autonomous racing application, a supervised baseline trained without sensor failures may cause the vehicle to leave the track. In contrast, a model trained using the proposed masking scheme enables reliable racing performance in the presence of sensor failures.
